source_document.body:
Only 25% of procurement leaders have redesigned jobs because of AI , even as 63% of senior procurement leaders expect the technology to greatly improve performance over the next three years, according to findings by Gartner .
What’s Related
The firm warned that the gap could leave procurement teams with employees whose skills no longer match their work. As AI takes over routine tasks, leaders need to decide how responsibilities will change and help employees prepare.
The findings came from two surveys completed in April 2026. Gartner’s Chief Procurement Officer Survey included 213 senior procurement leaders, while its C-Suite AI Survey included 1,303 respondents across business functions, including 134 procurement leaders.
“Successful AI implementation at the functional level is fundamentally a role redesign challenge,” said Fareen Mehrzai, senior director analyst in Gartner’s Supply Chain practice. “Responsibilities and skills across procurement are already changing. Chief procurement officers (CPOs) who delay redesigning roles risk leaving employees without a clear path forward and their organizations without the talent needed to capture the full value from AI.”
RELATED STORIES: Why Procurement Teams Need Rules Before Giving AI More Power | Agentic AI Is Changing Procurement. Governance Must Keep Up
Routine work faces the most pressure
Gartner said middle-skilled procurement roles face particular pressure because much of their work follows standardized steps that AI can handle. It expects demand to shift toward lower-skilled positions that rely heavily on AI assistance and higher-skilled jobs requiring creativity and complex problem-solving.
The firm recommends reviewing roles with employees to determine which responsibilities should remain with people and which should move to AI. Without that planning, Gartner said, organizations risk lower employee morale,skill gaps, and weaker competitiveness.
Assessing technical and human skills
Gartner also urged procurement leaders to regularly assess both employees’ technical knowledge and their human skills. The firm said creativity, influence, adaptability, and ethical judgment become more valuable as routine work is automate d .
The firm recommends providing focused training before those skills weaken. That means preparing employees for changing responsibilities alongside teaching them how to use AI tools.
Let employees test new ways of working
The third recommendation is to give employees a safe place to try AI tools and new workflows, with failed experiments treated as part of learning. Gartner said leaders should explain their AI goals, address employee resistance directly, and help colleagues learn from one another.
“CPOs must give employees agency in shaping how their roles evolve and create an environment where they can build new capabilities through experimentation,” said Mehrzai. “Role redesign cannot be a one-time exercise; it will need continuous adjustment as AI advances and employees learn what works in practice.”
